title: Neighbors in al-Andalus
hookLine: Muslims, Jews and Christians shared cities and learning, alongside real tension and times of persecution

lines: A JEWISH VIZIER WRITES A POEM.
HIS SON'S STORY IS THE OTHER FACE.
cards: A general sits in an army camp and writes a poem. In Hebrew. He is Samuel ibn Naghrela, a Jew who serves a Muslim king of Granada as vizier, the chief minister, and leads that king's troops in the field.
His Hebrew poems move in the meters of Arabic verse, and some were written on campaign: the night before a battle, the fear, the thanks for coming home alive.
A Jewish commander, a Muslim court, Hebrew words in Arabic rhythms. That's one face of al-Andalus. His son's story shows the other, and today needs both.

teach.b: Start with the frame. The Qur'an calls Jews and Christians People of the Book, and under Muslim rule in al-Andalus they lived as protected communities, with their own worship, clergy and courts.
They also paid a special tax and lived under limits a Muslim neighbor didn't. Protection and inequality, in the same arrangement. Now the sharing.

At the court of Abd al-Rahman the Third, a Jewish physician named Hasdai ibn Shaprut served as a trusted diplomat. Jewish poets, Samuel among them, wrote Hebrew verse in the patterns of Arabic poetry.
Philosophers of all three communities argued over the same Greek books, read in Arabic. Now the other side, said just as plainly.
In Cordoba, some Christians who publicly denounced Islam were executed, and their community remembered them as martyrs.
In Granada, a mob turned on the city's Jews, and among the dead was the vizier Joseph, Samuel's own son.

teach.h: MARTYRS, A MOB, A FAMILY THAT FLED.
teach.b: Later, under the Almohads, Jews and Christians faced pressure to convert, and some fled; the family of the Jewish scholar Maimonides was among them. Christian kingdoms to the north, meanwhile, pushed south by war.
So which was it, harmony or persecution? Both, at different times, in different cities, under different rulers.

teach.h: THAT YE MAY KNOW ONE ANOTHER.
teach.b: The Qur'an gives a reason for difference, in Pickthall's words: "We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another." Knowing one another includes the hard chapters.

how: Muslims, Jews and Christians today remember al-Andalus in different ways; historians describe both its shared learning and its inequality and episodes of violence.

o: a Jewish vizier of Granada who wrote Hebrew poems
a Jewish physician who served as Cordoba's diplomat
a Christian martyr of Cordoba remembered by his church

games.q: who's who in the story — tap the pairs.
p: Jewish vizier of Granada and Hebrew poet
Jewish diplomat at the caliph's court
the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians

s: al-Andalus was a perfect paradise of harmony
Jews and Christians were protected but not equal, and there were executions, a mob in Granada and forced conversions.
there was real sharing too: a Jewish diplomat at court, Hebrew poems in Arabic patterns, scholars reading the same books.
a Jewish vizier of Granada also led its troops and wrote Hebrew poems
Samuel ibn Naghrela served a Muslim king as vizier and commander, and wrote Hebrew verse in Arabic meters.

games.q: you're Samuel ibn Naghrela, a Jew serving a Muslim king of Granada, back from a campaign. you want to write about it. how do you write?
o: in Latin, like the churchmen to the north.
in Hebrew, in the meters of Arabic poetry.
not at all; a vizier doesn't write poems.
games.why: Hebrew, shaped by Arabic meters. his poems show how close the neighbors' cultures had come; his son Joseph's death at the hands of a Granada mob shows how fragile it was.

practice: Bring to mind a neighbor, coworker or classmate whose family comes from a story different from yours, and let one honest question form: how did their people come to be here, what did they carry, what did they lose?
If you pray, remember them in your prayer; if you don't, hold them in mind with good will.

wordCard.voice: Ibn Naghrela, the Jewish vizier and general who served a Muslim king of Granada and wrote Hebrew poems in Arabic meters, even on campaign. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: People of the Book, the Qur'an's name for Jews and Christians.

carryVoice: Your line: shared, and not simple. The easy summary is rarely the whole story. Nine hundred forty-two days now.
